component.noExposed: Nothing exposed through a template ref.
component.a11yPattern: Follows the {pattern} pattern from the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide.
component.a11yNoKeys: It has no keyboard interaction of its own.

home.headline: Components that compile straight to Vapor, not around it.
home.tagline: 60+ components for Vue 3, with one motion system built in. One source compiles to both the VDOM build and Vue Vapor.
home.featureVaporTitle: A real Vapor build, not a shim
home.featureVaporBody: Every component compiles through Vue 3.6’s Vapor mode from the same source.
home.featureAnimationBody: Every component ships its own motion. Tune it with the motion prop and springs, or animate any part with GSAP or motion.
home.featureI18nBody: Every built-in string translates through your own i18n instance.
home.featurePrimitivesBody: No compound components to assemble and no hidden context to wire up.
home.featureSsrBody: Every component checks for a browser before it touches window or document, so it renders in Nuxt, server-rendered apps and static site generators. This docs site is built with Vite SSG from the same components.
home.featureSkillBody: A companion package that gives Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex and other agents every component’s real API. It’s generated from vael-ui’s own types, not written by hand.

gettingStarted.title: Getting started
gettingStarted.intro: vael-ui is a Vue 3 component library with a full Vue Vapor build. Every component animates through one motion system, and you can animate any part with your own library instead.
gettingStarted.vaporIntro: Both builds ship in the same package, from the same source, with the same props. Pick the one your app runs. Every component page has a toggle to compare them.
gettingStarted.vaporPinIntro: The Vapor build needs Vue 3.6, which is still a prerelease. Install the exact version vael-ui is built against, {version}. A range such as ^3.5.0 can install Vue 3.5, which has no Vapor mode, and another prerelease can break the compiled components:
gettingStarted.vaporAppIntro: A Vapor app starts with createVaporApp and imports components, composables and directives from 'vael-ui/vapor'. Your own components opt in with <script setup vapor>:
gettingStarted.vaporForceIntro: To skip the vapor attribute in every file, turn on features.vapor in {'@'}vitejs/plugin-vue 6.0.8 or later. Every <script setup> component in your app then compiles as Vapor:
gettingStarted.vaporMixIntro: A VDOM app can also host Vapor components, so you can move an existing app to Vapor a few components at a time. Keep createApp, install Vue’s vaporInteropPlugin, and import from 'vael-ui/vapor' in the components you mark vapor. For a new app, pick one build instead. A component marked vapor imports directives such as vTooltip from 'vael-ui/vapor' too, because app.directive only registers them for VDOM components.
gettingStarted.installIntro: vael-ui is on npm. Install it with your package manager:
gettingStarted.usageImportNote: Each component imports its own styles. Add this import only if you’re on a version before 0.2.0 or want all styles loaded at once. See {link} for base-style setup.
gettingStarted.usageIntro: Import components from 'vael-ui' for the VDOM build. For the Vapor build (Vue 3.6’s mode without a virtual DOM), import from 'vael-ui/vapor'. The props are the same in both:
gettingStarted.fontIntro: Components use the font of the page around them and ship none of their own. Without one, the browser falls back to its default serif font, so set a font on body:
gettingStarted.darkModeIntro: Dark mode is CSS only. It follows <html data-theme="dark"> and falls back to prefers-color-scheme. vael-ui ships no toggle, but useColorScheme() tracks changes to the OS setting and saves the choice through the persist option you pass:
gettingStarted.appearanceHeadIntro: If you save the color mode or an app-wide font size in localStorage, put this script in your HTML <head>, before the app bundle. It restores both before the first paint. Save a CSS font size such as 13px or 1rem under app-font-size. Components inherit it unless you set a scoped theme.fontSize.
gettingStarted.directivesIntro: v-tooltip, v-scroll-mask and v-hover-indicator aren’t registered globally by default. If you use any of them in more than one component, register them once:
gettingStarted.directivesNote: v-tooltip also needs one <TooltipHost /> mounted in your app. In a Vapor app, import both directives from vael-ui/vapor instead.
gettingStarted.ssrIntro: Both builds render on the server and hydrate in the browser. {link} sets up everything below for you.
gettingStarted.ssrNoExternal: With plain Vite server rendering, let Vite bundle vael-ui for the server. Each component imports its own CSS, and Node can’t load CSS files on its own:
gettingStarted.ssrTeleports: Dialogs, popovers, toasts and tooltips render into <body> through <Teleport>. Vue returns that HTML separately, in ctx.teleports. Add it at the start of <body>, before your app’s element, or the page won’t hydrate cleanly:
gettingStarted.ssrLocale: Set locale on ConfigProvider when you render on a server. Without it, dates, numbers and the first day of the week follow the server’s language, then change once the page runs in the browser.

globalSetup.title: Global setup
globalSetup.intro: vael-ui has four singletons: components you mount once, anywhere in your app, for every other component to use.
globalSetup.tooltipHostIntro: Renders every v-tooltip. If it isn’t mounted, tooltips never appear, and no error tells you why.
globalSetup.tooltipHostOptions: It takes the same options that each tooltip can override:
globalSetup.dialogHostIntro: Renders dialogs you open from code with openDialog() or confirmAction(). A <Dialog v-model:open> in your own template doesn’t need it. It has no props or configuration.
globalSetup.popoverHostIntro: Renders popovers you open from code with openPopover(), or with confirmAction() and surface: 'popover'. A <Popover v-model:open> in your own template doesn’t need it. It has no props or configuration.
globalSetup.toasterIntro: Renders the toasts that {code} creates. It has its own props, so it’s documented on {link}.
globalSetup.allTogetherIntro: Mount all four once, in your app’s root template:

tailwind.layerNote: vael-ui ships in {layer}. Tailwind v4 puts its utilities in a layer too, so import order matters. Import vael-ui’s CSS before your Tailwind entry, as shown below, so its layer registers first. Tailwind’s utilities then come later in the cascade, and a Tailwind utility on a vael-ui component always wins, with no {important} or specificity fights. See {link} for how layers work.
tailwind.orderWarning: Each component loads its own CSS, so vael-ui needs no stylesheet import, except with Tailwind v4. Its utilities live in their own cascade layer, and the first stylesheet that names a layer sets the order. Import vael-ui/layers.css before your Tailwind entry, in your app’s main entry file. It only names vael-ui’s layer and loads no component CSS, so the order holds as components load their CSS later.
tailwind.mergingIntro: Every component takes a ui prop for part classes, such as :ui="{'{'} root: 'my-class' {'}'}". To resolve conflicting Tailwind utilities there the way tailwind-merge does, where the last one wins per property, set it up once:
tailwind.mergingNote: Every ui.* part class in the tree now goes through twMerge.

stylingLayers.title: Styling and cascade layers
stylingLayers.intro: vael-ui ships in {layer}. Unlayered CSS always beats layered CSS, whatever its specificity, so an unlayered base reset overrides vael-ui’s styles without any warning. To prevent that, put your base styles in a layer too, and order that layer first.
stylingLayers.orderNote: Here, import order only sets the layer position. An unlayered override always wins, wherever it loads.
stylingLayers.bundlerNote: Each component imports its own styles. Add the import below only if you’re on a version before 0.2.0 or want all styles loaded at once.
stylingLayers.overrideNote: When you override one component on purpose, with the {code} prop or a Tailwind utility, you want your rule to win. Keep that CSS unlayered, as it is by default. See {link}.
stylingLayers.cssVariablesIntro: vael-ui’s colors, radii, shadows and default motion timings come from CSS custom properties. Override any of them in your own unlayered stylesheet:
stylingLayers.cssVariablesThemeNote: ConfigProvider’s theme sets primary, danger, radius and fontSize. Without fontSize, components follow your html font size, form fields included. If that’s under 16 px, call preventFocusZoom() once so iPhones don’t zoom into fields. Set the other tokens with CSS.

rows.primary: Primary action color: buttons, links and focus accents.
rows.primaryContrast: Text and icon color on top of primary.
rows.contrastVariant: Text and icon color on top of this color.
rows.surface: Base background for panels, cards and dialogs.
rows.borderStrong: Stronger border color for emphasized edges.
rows.overlay: Backdrop color behind dialogs and other modals.
rows.radius: Base corner radius for controls such as buttons, inputs and badges.
rows.radiusSurface: Corner radius for large surfaces such as panels, cards and tables. It’s capped, so a large radius doesn’t turn them into pills.
rows.zPopover: Stacking order for popovers, menus and selects.
rows.zTooltip: Stacking order for tooltips, the topmost layer.
rows.easeOut: Default easing for elements entering and settling.
rows.easeInOut: Easing for movement on screen, such as resizing and repositioning.
rows.easeDrawer: Easing for slides from an edge, such as drawers and sheets.
rows.durationDrawer: How long a drawer or sheet takes to slide open.
rows.durationIndicator: How long the hover highlight in lists and menus takes to glide to the next row.
rows.durationIndicatorWide: The same glide for the wide rows of MenuList, Tree and DataTable.
rows.indicatorBg: Color of the hover highlight. Set it instead of a row’s :hover background, which would paint over the highlight.
rows.toastOffset: Distance from the screen edge to the toast stack.
rows.joinFrame: Goes on your control’s bordered element, not on Field. Optional value: sm, md or lg.
rows.joinStart: A cell or an attached label sits on the control’s start edge.
rows.joinEnd: A cell or an attached label sits on the control’s end edge.
rows.joinAttached: Field draws the label as a joined cell.
rows.cellBg: Background of joined cells: an attached label, #prepend and #append.
rows.labelWidth: Width of a start or end label. Set it on a parent to line up a whole form.

stylingLayers.joinTitle: Joining your own control to a Field
stylingLayers.joinIntro: A Field’s attached label and its #prepend and #append cells join the control’s bordered frame. vael-ui’s own controls mark that frame with data-ui-frame. Add the same attribute to your own control, and it joins too. Set it to the control’s size (sm, md or lg), and the cells match its corner radius and font size.
stylingLayers.joinLayerNote: Field’s join rules are in {layer}, so your control’s own unlayered styles win over them. In that case, flatten the corners and recolor the border yourself, with the attributes Field sets on its root:
stylingLayers.joinCellNote: Give a control inside a cell its own aria-label. It stands alone, so the Field’s label doesn’t name it.
stylingLayers.advancedNote: Most apps don’t need this. It’s for building your own controls that plug into vael-ui.

animation.title: Customize motion
animation.intro: Every component that animates has built-in motion and a motion prop. Keep the built-in motion, turn it off, change its values, or run it with GSAP, motion or the Web Animations API.
animation.builtInIntro: Leave motion unset and the component uses its built-in motion. Most apps need nothing more. Set it to false and the component changes state at once: it still opens, closes and removes items, without animating.
animation.builtInProvider: To turn motion off everywhere, such as in screenshot tests, set :motion="false" on a ConfigProvider. Under reduced motion, the built-in motion keeps its fades and drops its movement.
animation.kindsCheck: Each component exports its own motion type, such as DialogMotion, that lists its parts and states. The part names match its ui keys. For a list, the name in parentheses is the part each item gets.
animation.valuesIntro: Pass an object to describe the motion as data. initial sets where each part comes in from, and exit sets where it leaves to. The keys are part names, and the values are CSS properties plus x, y and blur.
animation.valuesTiming: For timing, give a spring, or a duration in milliseconds with an easing, not both. A spring’s damping of 1 settles without overshoot, and lower values overshoot. response is roughly the seconds it takes to arrive. Leave out exit and the part fades out with a slight shrink.
animation.hooksIntro: When values aren’t enough, add enter(parts, ctx) and leave(parts, ctx) hooks. parts holds the component’s elements by part name. Return what your library returns: a Web Animations Animation, a GSAP tween or timeline, the controls from motion’s animate(), or a promise. The component waits for it before it finishes opening or removes the element.
animation.hooksInterrupt: If the motion is interrupted, such as a close while it’s still opening, the component stops what you returned with kill, stop or cancel, and aborts ctx.signal. Under reduced motion, hooks don’t run. Set reducedMotion: 'run' to run them anyway, and check ctx.reducedMotion yourself.
animation.gsapExampleIntro: Return a timeline. Here a Dialog fades its overlay and slides its panel:
animation.motionExampleIntro: Return the controls from animate(), imported from motion-v or motion. Here a Popover panel springs in:
animation.waapiExampleIntro: No library needed: element.animate() returns an Animation. Here a Message slides out to the side when it closes:
animation.listsIntro: Toaster, Timeline, FileUpload, SpeedDial and DataTable take the same motion object for their items. CommandPalette takes it under items, and Select, Combobox and CascadeSelect under chips. Values and hooks apply to each item. A hook gets one item’s parts, such as {'{'} toast {'}'}, {'{'} item {'}'}, {'{'} row {'}'}, {'{'} action {'}'} or {'{'} chip {'}'}, plus ctx.index for your own stagger.
animation.listsOptions: Lists take three more keys. stagger is the seconds between items that arrive together. leaving sets what happens to a leaving item’s space: with 'pop', the default, the other items close the gap at once; with 'hold', the item keeps its space until it’s gone. appear: true also animates the items already there when the list mounts.
animation.listsHooksIntro: With hooks, each Timeline step gets its marker, connectors and content:
animation.listsEvents: The old list events, such as {'@'}item-enter and {'@'}item-leave, are gone. Move that code into enter and leave.
animation.guardsIntro: beforeClose is a guard. Return true to close, false to stay open, or a promise of either. While the promise is pending, the overlay stays open and still. A confirmation takes one line:
animation.guardsExit: The guard receives the reason for closing. It doesn’t run your exit animation: put that in motion.leave. The done() callback is gone.
animation.forceMountIntro: forceMount keeps the content mounted while it’s closed and toggles it with v-show. Use it when the content must stay in the DOM, such as to keep its state or to measure it. The built-in motion doesn’t play on content kept this way, so it shows and hides at once. To animate it, use motion hooks.
animation.appWideTitle: One style for the whole app
animation.appWideIntro: Pass a style to ConfigProvider to set motion once. Role keys, such as overlay and list, apply to every component of that kind. Component keys, such as dialog and toaster, override their role. A component’s own motion prop overrides both. version: 1 marks the format, so a saved style keeps working in later releases.
animation.vAnimateTitle: Animate your own elements with v-animate
animation.vAnimateIntro: The v-animate directive gives your own elements the same motion. v-animate="{'{'} initial: {'{'} opacity: 0, y: 8 {'}'} {'}'}" plays when the element mounts. When it unmounts, it leaves the way it came, a little quieter and quicker.
animation.vAnimateNamed: Inside a component, add a name: v-animate:rows joins that component’s motion as a target called rows. The element enters and leaves with the panel. Set its values on the element, or under targets.rows in the component’s motion.
animation.exposedIntro: For full control over one part, set :motion="false", put a template ref on the component, and animate its DOM elements: el for the root, plus parts such as checkEl or thumbEl. Each component’s Exposed table lists what it has.
animation.exposedExampleIntro: In this example, GSAP pops the check mark in each time the box is checked:

descriptions.ConfigProvider: A wrapper that sets the theme, size, language, class merging and motion for every component inside it. Use it at the root of your app to set them once.
descriptions.Button: A button for an action, with variants, sizes, icons and a loading state. Use it for any action, and add hold when a destructive one needs a press and hold to confirm.
descriptions.SplitButton: A main action joined to a chevron that opens related actions in a dropdown. Use it when one action is the usual choice and a few others belong beside it.
descriptions.Toolbar: A strip of related controls with arrow-key focus and an overflow menu for what doesn’t fit. Use it to group the actions for one view or one editor.
descriptions.SpeedDial: A floating action button that fans out into secondary actions. Use it when a screen has one main button and a few related actions.
descriptions.Dial: A wheel you turn to change a number, with no end stops unless you set min or max. Use it for open-ended values and fine adjustments.
descriptions.SelectButton: A segmented control that picks one or more values from a short list. Use it instead of radios or checkboxes when every option fits in one row.
descriptions.Input: A single-line text field with sizes, states, and start and end slots for icons or buttons. Use it for names, emails, search and other short text.
descriptions.Textarea: A multi-line text field that can grow with its content. Use it for comments, notes and other long text.
descriptions.InputNumber: A number field with steppers and locale-aware formatting and parsing. Use it for quantities, prices and percentages.
descriptions.OtpInput: A row of single-character boxes for a one-time code, with paste and auto-advance. Use it for sign-in and verification codes.
descriptions.Editable: Text that turns into an input when you click it, and saves on Enter or blur. Use it to rename something in place.
descriptions.ColorPicker: A swatch that opens a picker with a saturation and brightness plane, a hue slider, a hex field, optional presets and an eyedropper where supported. Use it when any color is allowed, not only a few.
descriptions.PasswordInput: A password field with a reveal button and a requirements hint. Use it on sign-up and sign-in forms.
descriptions.Checkbox: A box for one yes or no choice, with an optional indeterminate state. Use it when each choice is independent of the others.
descriptions.Radio: One option in a set where only one can be selected. Use it only inside a RadioGroup.
descriptions.RadioGroup: A group of Radio options where only one can be selected at a time. Use it for a short list of choices that should all stay visible.
descriptions.Switch: An on and off toggle styled like a physical switch. Use it for settings that take effect at once.
descriptions.Slider: A track with one thumb for a value, or two for a range. Use it to pick a number by dragging.
descriptions.Knob: A rotary control that sets a number within a fixed arc. Use it for bounded values, such as a volume or a level.
descriptions.Field: A wrapper that connects a label, help text and an error message to a form control. Use it to label a control without wiring its id and ARIA attributes yourself.
descriptions.DatePicker: A text field with a calendar popover for picking a date, a range or a time. Use it in forms where people type or pick a date.
descriptions.Calendar: A month grid for picking a single date or a date range. Use it when the calendar should stay on the page.
descriptions.FileUpload: A drop zone and file list for picking files, with validation. Use it for attachments and uploads in forms.
descriptions.Rating: A row of stars you click, drag or set with the arrow keys, with optional half steps. Use it for reviews and feedback.
descriptions.Select: A dropdown for picking one or more values from a list, with filtering and virtualization. Use it when a list is too long for radios or a SelectButton.
descriptions.Combobox: A searchable dropdown that also accepts free text. Use it for autocomplete, or for tags people create as they type.
descriptions.CascadeSelect: A dropdown for picking a path through nested options, one level at a time. Use it for categories or places that branch into smaller ones.
descriptions.Tree: An indented, collapsible list for nested data, with single or multiple selection. Use it for file explorers and nested navigation.
descriptions.TreeSelect: A dropdown with a Tree in its panel, for picking one or more nodes from a hierarchy. Use it when a form field takes a value from nested data.
descriptions.Dialog: A modal window over the page that waits until someone responds or dismisses it. Use it for a task or a decision that needs an answer first.
descriptions.Drawer: A panel that slides in from an edge of the screen. Use it for navigation, filters or details beside the page.
descriptions.Popover: A floating panel anchored to a trigger element. Use it for short forms, pickers or extra detail.
descriptions.Tooltip: A short label that appears on hover or focus. Use it to name an icon button or explain a control.
descriptions.BottomSheet: A panel that slides up from the bottom edge and snaps to the heights you set. Use it on touch screens, where people drag it up, down or away.
descriptions.ContextMenu: A menu that opens at the pointer on right-click, or on a long press on touch screens. Use it for actions on the item under the pointer.
descriptions.Tour: A guided walkthrough that highlights one element at a time next to a callout. Use it for onboarding and product tours.
descriptions.Menu: A dropdown list of actions that opens from a trigger, with full keyboard navigation. Use it for a set of actions behind one button.
descriptions.MenuList: Menu’s rows rendered in the page instead of a dropdown. Use it for a sidebar or settings navigation that stays on screen.
descriptions.Tabs: A row of tabs that switches between panels, with a sliding indicator under the active tab. Use it to split related content into views on one page.
descriptions.Toaster: The container that shows the notifications toast() creates. Mount it once, anywhere in your app.
descriptions.Message: An inline banner for status text: info, success, warning or error. Use it for a notice that stays in the page.
descriptions.Progress: A bar or ring for a task’s progress, known or unknown, or for stacked shares of a whole with a legend. Use it for uploads, long tasks or a storage breakdown.
descriptions.Loader: A small spinner in five styles that sizes to the text around it. Use it to show that something is in progress.
descriptions.Skeleton: A placeholder shape that stands in for content while it loads. Use it when you know the layout before the data arrives.
descriptions.DataTable: A data grid with sorting, selection, column resizing and virtualization, built from Column components. Use it for records people sort, select and compare.
descriptions.Column: One column of a DataTable. Use it only inside a DataTable.
descriptions.Pagination: Page-number controls that split a long list or table across pages. Use it when people need to reach a specific page.
descriptions.Card: A bordered container that groups related content, with an optional title and actions. Use it for a summary, a setting or a link to more.
descriptions.Avatar: A circular or square image, or initials, that represents a person or an entity. Use it beside names in lists, comments and headers.
descriptions.Badge: A small dot, count or label for status or something new. Use it in the badge slot of a Button or an Avatar to pin it to a corner.
descriptions.Tag: A compact label that categorizes or annotates an item inline. Use it for statuses, categories and keywords.
descriptions.Chip: A compact token, optionally removable, for selected filters, tags or values. Use it to show choices people can take back.
descriptions.Kbd: A keyboard key or shortcut, styled like a physical key. Use it in hints and help text.
descriptions.AnimatedNumber: A number whose changed digits roll to their new value, formatted for any locale. Use it for counters, prices and stats that change on screen.
descriptions.AnimatedText: Text that swaps to the next with a short fade and lift, while its width eases so nothing beside it jumps. Use it for labels and statuses that change in place.
descriptions.Timeline: An ordered list of steps joined by a line, where each step can hold any content. Use it for a history, an order’s progress or a changelog.
descriptions.Accordion: A stack of collapsible sections where opening one can close the others. Use it for FAQs or long content split into sections.
descriptions.AccordionItem: One collapsible section of an Accordion. Use it only inside an Accordion.
descriptions.Collapsible: A single section that shows and hides its content. Use it for optional or secondary content.
descriptions.Separator: A thin line, with an optional label, that divides content into groups. Use it between sections, or with a label such as “or” between two choices.
descriptions.Resizable: A drag handle that resizes a panel between a minimum and a maximum size. Use it for sidebars and split views.
descriptions.SwipeToReveal: A row you swipe to reveal actions underneath it, like a native mobile list row. Use it for actions such as archive or delete on touch screens.
descriptions.Sortable: A list you reorder by dragging or from the keyboard. Use it for any order people set by hand, in one list or across several.
descriptions.PullToRefresh: A pull-down gesture at the top of a scroll container that starts a refresh. Use it for feeds and lists on touch screens.
descriptions.Dock: A macOS-style row of icons that magnify as the pointer or a finger moves over them. Use it for app-style navigation or a launcher.
descriptions.BreadcrumbItem: One link, or the current page, in a Breadcrumb trail. Use it only inside a Breadcrumb.
descriptions.BreadcrumbSeparator: The divider between two BreadcrumbItems, a chevron unless you pass your own content. Use it only inside a Breadcrumb.
descriptions.ButtonGroup: A connected row or column of buttons that can also work as single or multiple toggles. Use it for related actions or options that belong together.
descriptions.CommandPalette: A searchable list of commands in a dialog, opened from a button or a keyboard shortcut such as ⌘K. Use it to let people reach any action or page from the keyboard.
descriptions.Stepper: A sequence of steps that shows progress and lets people move between them. Use it for checkouts, sign-up flows and setup wizards.
descriptions.Breadcrumb: A trail of links from the top of the site down to the current page. Use it on pages deep in a hierarchy.
descriptions.AvatarGroup: Several avatars stacked into one overlapping row, with a count for the ones that don’t fit. Use it to show who belongs to a team, a chat or a document.
descriptions.ScrollArea: A scroll box with slim, themed scrollbars and faded edges, in one or both directions. Use it for panels and lists that scroll inside the page.

pageNotes.Resizable: This site’s sidebar is built with Resizable. Drag its right edge to try it.
pageNotes.ContextMenu: Keyboard users open the menu with Shift+F10 or the Menu key, which fire contextmenu on the focused element. Make the wrapped target focusable (tabindex="0") and give it an accessible name.
pageNotes.Tree: Rows update from reactive state. In a custom #node slot, read reactive values (props, refs, computeds), not plain variables captured from the parent.
pageNotes.DataTable: For hundreds of rows, add virtualize and a scroll-height, such as scroll-height="400px". The table then draws only the rows in view, so sorting, selecting and scrolling stay fast. Past 150 rendered rows, rows also stop sliding into place as they sort.

i18nKeys.title: Translating vael-ui
i18nKeys.intro: Every built-in string, such as the dialog close button, toast dismiss and empty states, has an English default. To translate them, pass your own i18n instance to ConfigProvider. It reads from your existing catalog under the uiKit namespace, so there’s nothing extra to install. Keys you haven’t translated show the English default. If you translate some keys but not all, development builds log one warning per locale that lists the missing ones.
i18nKeys.copyIntro: Copy this into your locale files under the uiKit key, then translate the values:

autoImport.title: Auto import
autoImport.intro: vael-ui/resolver is a resolver for unplugin-vue-components. Register it once, and you can use any vael-ui component in a template without importing it. It resolves components, not directives.
autoImport.setupIntro: Add the resolver wherever unplugin-vue-components is already configured:
autoImport.setupOutro: Write the tag, and the plugin adds the import at build time:
autoImport.vaporIntro: vael-ui ships two builds from the same source: the VDOM build and the Vapor build (vael-ui/vapor). The resolver imports from the VDOM build by default. Pass variant: 'vapor' to import from the Vapor build instead. The resolver imports every component from one build, so pick the one your app renders with.
autoImport.vaporHostsNote: In a Vapor template, unplugin-vue-components only finds components inside another component’s slot. Until it supports Vapor, import top-level ones by hand, such as <Toaster>, <DialogHost> and <ConfigProvider>.
autoImport.oneImportIntro: Your editor’s auto-import may keep suggesting vael-ui instead of vael-ui/vapor. It’s a known TypeScript limitation when a package exports the same name from two entry points. To avoid it, set a vapor export condition instead of importing from the subpath. Every import … from 'vael-ui' then resolves to the Vapor build across the project, for components and composables alike, so auto-import can’t pick the wrong one.
autoImport.oneImportDefaults: Add vapor to Vite’s default conditions instead of replacing them. A bare ['vapor'] drops the defaults, and other packages can then load the wrong file. The ssr line does the same for server rendering.
autoImport.oneImportNote: The Vite condition sets which build loads, and the TypeScript condition keeps the types in line with it. If you set only one, nothing errors: you get the right types with the wrong build, or the reverse.
autoImport.cssIntro: No extra setup here. Every vael-ui component imports its own CSS, so resolving a component also loads its styles. Most unplugin-vue-components resolvers need a separate sideEffects entry for that.
autoImport.bundlersIntro: unplugin-vue-components supports Vite, Webpack, Rollup, esbuild and Rspack. The resolver is a plain function, so it works the same with all of them.

nuxt.title: Nuxt
nuxt.intro: vael-ui/nuxt is a Nuxt module. Add it once, and you can use any vael-ui component in a template without importing it. It uses Nuxt’s own component registration, not unplugin-vue-components.
nuxt.setupIntro: Register the module in your Nuxt config:
nuxt.setupOutro: Write the tag, and Nuxt resolves the import for you:
nuxt.appSetupIntro: The module doesn’t mount the hosts. Mount the ones you use once in app.vue. {link} explains what each one does.
nuxt.composablesIntro: Composables such as toast() and openDialog() aren’t auto-imported. Import them from 'vael-ui', or from 'vael-ui/vapor' with the Vapor variant:
nuxt.directivesIntro: The module registers v-animate for you, but not v-tooltip, v-scroll-mask or v-hover-indicator. Register those in a plugin. With the Vapor variant, import them from 'vael-ui/vapor':
nuxt.excludeIntro: Skip specific component names, such as to register your own <Button> under the same tag:
nuxt.vaporIntro: Set variant: 'vapor' to use vael-ui/vapor, the same option vael-ui/resolver takes. The module turns on Nuxt’s vue.vapor for you. It needs Nuxt 4.6 or later and Vue 3.6. Pin Vue to the exact version given in Getting started.
nuxt.vaporOutro: Pages still render on the server. The server renders each component to HTML, and the browser hydrates it as a Vapor component, with nothing else to configure.
nuxt.vaporForceIntro: To compile your own <script setup> components as Vapor too, without adding vapor to each one, turn on {'@'}vitejs/plugin-vue’s features.vapor through Nuxt’s vite.vue:
nuxt.resolverIntro: If your Nuxt app already uses unplugin-vue-components to auto-import other libraries, use vael-ui/resolver instead. See the {link} guide.

skill.title: AI agent skill
skill.intro: A companion package that teaches AI coding agents to use vael-ui. It works with Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Codex, Cursor and others. It covers every component’s props, slots and events, every composable, and how to set up motion, theming and the VDOM and Vapor builds. It’s generated from vael-ui’s own types and docs, not written by hand, so it stays accurate as vael-ui changes. It’s versioned and released separately from vael-ui.
skill.claudeCodeIntro: Add the marketplace once, then install the skill:
skill.otherAgentsIntro: Any agent that supports the shared Agent Skills spec can install it with skill.sh. That includes GitHub Copilot, Codex, Cursor and more than 70 others:

skill.includedComponents: Every component’s props, slots, events and exposed refs
skill.includedComposables: Every standalone composable’s parameters, return values and usage examples
skill.includedAnimation: The motion system (the motion prop, enter and leave hooks, v-animate), with GSAP and motion examples

composableDescriptions.confirmAction: A confirm step, shown as a centered dialog or a popover anchored to a trigger, that waits for your async handler before it closes. Use it before an action that’s hard to undo.
composableDescriptions.useDialogService: Opens any component as a dialog from code instead of markup. Its result promise resolves with the value the dialog closes with. Use it for dialogs you open from a function.
composableDescriptions.usePopoverService: Opens any component as an anchored popover from code instead of markup. Its result promise resolves with the value the popover closes with. Use it for popovers you open from a function.
composableDescriptions.useToast: Shows toast notifications from anywhere in your app, with variant shortcuts and a promise helper that swaps a loading toast for success or error. Use it for feedback that shouldn’t interrupt the page.
composableDescriptions.useTour: The step and group navigation behind Tour, as headless state with no DOM or rendering. Use it to build your own tour.
composableDescriptions.useAsyncLoading: Tracks every async task you run through it, and stays loading until all of them settle. Use it for one loading state over several requests.
composableDescriptions.useNumberFormat: Formats and parses numbers for a locale with the same options, so typed text and its formatted display always match. Use it for your own number fields, or to give AnimatedNumber the same format.
composableDescriptions.useColorScheme: Switches between light, dark and system modes, and can spread the new scheme in a circle from a click. Use it for a theme toggle, and pass your own storage functions to remember the choice.
composableDescriptions.useHaptic: Plays haptic feedback on phones that support it: a light tick, a bump, a short success, warning or error pattern, or your own. Use it for moments that commit something.
composableDescriptions.springEasing: Turns a spring into a CSS linear() curve and its settle time. Use it to give element.animate() or a CSS transition the same spring as vael-ui.
composableDescriptions.preventFocusZoom: Stops iOS from zooming in when a form field gets focus, so fields can match the rest of your text size. Call it once on the client, such as in main.ts.
composableDescriptions.useFloatingPosition: The positioning engine behind Popover, Menu and Tooltip, built on Floating UI. Use it to build your own anchored panels.
composableDescriptions.useVirtualizer: Renders only the visible rows of a long list, so the DOM stays small. Use it for your own long lists.
composableDescriptions.useFieldControl: Connects a custom form control to the nearest Field: its id, ARIA attributes, and focus and filled state. Use it when your own control sits inside a Field.
composableDescriptions.useHoverIndicator: The sliding hover and keyboard highlight behind vael-ui’s lists. Use it to give your own lists the same highlight.
composableDescriptions.useSpringValue: Interruptible spring physics in three forms: a reactive value, an imperative spring that writes each frame without re-rendering, and the pure step function behind both. Use it for motion that can change target partway.
composableDescriptions.useTabIndicator: The sliding selection indicator behind Tabs, SelectButton, MenuList and Pagination. Use it for your own segmented controls and lists.
composableDescriptions.useScrollLock: Locks scrolling on the page or any element without a layout shift, as dialogs do while they’re open. Use it for your own overlays and full-screen panels.
composableDescriptions.moveTreeNode: Moves a node and its subtree to a new parent and index, in place. An impossible move, such as a folder into itself, changes nothing. Use it to apply a drag-and-drop move to your tree data.
composableDescriptions.useFileDrop: Turns any element into a drop target for files, with a drag-over state that holds steady over child elements and ignores dragged text or links. Use it to build your own drop zone.

motionDocs.lede: Every vael-ui component animates with one motion system. Use the built-in motion as it is, change it with one motion prop, or run it with your own library.

motionDocs.propIntro: Every component takes motion. false turns its motion off. An object changes it: values for its parts, a spring or a duration, or enter and leave hooks for your own library.
motionDocs.propTable: Each component page has a Motion section that lists its parts, its states and its other motion options.
motionDocs.yoursIntro: v-animate gives your own elements the same motion: an entrance, an exit, a size that eases to fit its content, or a slide to a new place when the layout changes.
motionDocs.yoursComposables: For motion of your own, use the composables behind it:

composable.springEasing: Turns a spring into a CSS easing and its settle time.
composable.useSpringValue: A value that follows its target on a spring.
composable.useHoverIndicator: The sliding hover highlight, for your own lists.
composable.useTabIndicator: The sliding indicator behind Tabs and SelectButton.

springs.title: Springs and timing
springs.intro: A spring takes two numbers. damping sets how it settles: 1 stops without overshooting, and lower values bounce. response is roughly how long it takes, in seconds. A spring has no fixed duration, so you can interrupt it and reverse it from wherever it is.
springs.everywhereTitle: One spring for the whole app
springs.everywhereIntro: Set a spring on ConfigProvider, and the drawers, sheets, toasts, indicators and AnimatedNumber inside it all use that spring. The demos below follow the sliders above.
springs.drawerBody: This drawer opened on the spring you set.

engines.title: Your own engine
engines.intro: By default, vael-ui plays motion itself with CSS transitions and the Web Animations API, so transform and opacity run off the main thread. A style's engine plays overlay parts, list items and your own targets through a library you choose instead, with the same values and timing. States, swaps and linked elements always use the built-in engine.
engines.compareIntro: Three popovers with the same values, each inside its own ConfigProvider. Open them together to compare.

note.gsap: GSAP plays the values with its own easing.
note.motion: motion plays them with its own spring.

engines.adaptersIntro: An engine receives the element, the start and end values, and the timing in seconds, plus the spring behind it when there is one. Return what your library returns. vael-ui waits for it, and stops it if the animation is interrupted.
engines.appWideIntro: Put the adapter in the ConfigProvider at the root, and every component inside uses it. A component's own hooks still take priority.

gooey.label: Gooey
gooey.body: Blurred blobs that swell into shape

types.title: TypeScript
types.intro: Your editor knows every component's parts and states, every CSS property and vael-ui's timing tokens. A mistake turns red before you save.
types.completeIntro: Select a name in the code to see what your editor suggests there, then pick one to insert it.
types.completeHint: Select a dotted name to see what your editor suggests.
types.completeNote: The same names are listed in {link}.
types.mistakesIntro: vael-ui's own type tests check that each of these stays an error, so no release starts accepting one by accident.
types.unitsIntro: A plain number uses the unit shown. A string goes straight to CSS, so '2rem' and '50%' work too.
types.tokensIntro: duration and easing accept vael-ui's tokens, and your editor lists them. Below are their current values on this page. Pick a preset from the motion menu in the header, and the tokens a spring drives change with it.
types.warningsIntro: In development, vael-ui logs what went wrong and what to change. Production builds leave these messages out.
types.devtools: To see what moved and why, inspect the component. data-motion names the layers that set its motion, and each open and close shows on the Timings track of the Performance panel.

mistake.timing: A spring and a duration together
mistake.kind: A list option on a dialog

start.title: Getting started
start.intro: vael-ui components animate out of the box. You can change how they move for one component or for your whole app, with the same few options.

already.title: It already moves
already.body: Open the dialog, the select and the toast below. Every overlay, list and control has built-in motion. It stays short, and it closes faster than it opens.

one.title: Change one component
one.body: Every component takes a motion prop. Set where a part comes in from, such as initial: {'{'} panel: {'{'} y: 32 {'}'} {'}'}, and the spring it moves on.

timing.title: Timing
timing.body: Motion runs on a spring or on a duration. A spring takes a name, 'snappy', 'smooth', 'bouncy' or 'gentle', or its damping and response. A duration in ms takes any CSS easing, or one of vael-ui's by name, such as 'out', 'pop' or 'bounce', which lands like a dropped ball. On a spring, positions and sizes ride it, and opacity, colors and blur ease.

spring.title: One spring for everything
spring.body: Put a spring on ConfigProvider, and every component inside uses it. damping below 1 overshoots, and response is roughly how long it takes, in seconds. Or name it: 'snappy', 'smooth', 'bouncy' or 'gentle'.

off.title: Turn it off
off.body: :motion="false" on a component, or on ConfigProvider for everything inside, makes opening and closing instant. While motion is on, people who ask for reduced motion get the fades without the movement.

elements.title: Any element
elements.intro: Motion isn't only for vael-ui components. v-animate gives any of your elements an entrance and an exit, right in the template.

appear.title: In and out
appear.body: initial sets where the element comes in from. When Vue removes it, it leaves the way it came, faster and quieter, unless you give it an exit. Inside a component that closes, such as a dialog or a menu, it leaves with the panel instead. For the usual entrances, pick one by name: v-animate.fade, .rise, .drop, .pop or .blur. Add a spring the same way, as in v-animate.pop.bouncy, and tune it with a value: v-animate.rise="{'{'} delay: 0.1 {'}'}".

scroll.title: When it scrolls into view
scroll.body: when: 'visible' waits until the element is on screen, then plays once. Elements that share a name, such as v-animate:tiles, play in page order, one after another with a stagger. stagger: true spaces them by the stagger token; 'end', 'center' or 'edges' start the wave there instead.

replay.title: Play it again
replay.body: replay plays initial again each time its value changes, without remounting the element. Use it for a count going up, a status change or a failed copy. With appear: false, it plays only on those changes, not when the element mounts. With appear: 'later', what's there when the page first renders stays still, and anything added after comes in. Inside a component's panel, that's what's there when it opens.

layout.title: Slide to a new place
layout.body: layout: true slides an element to wherever the layout puts it, such as when a list reorders or a sibling grows. A delay waits before it slides, holding its old place meanwhile.

shared.title: From one place to another
shared.body: Two elements with the same layoutId act as one element. When one leaves and the other arrives, the new one grows out of the old one's box. Add layout: 'position' to keep its size on the way, so its text never stretches.

animate.title: Hold a look
animate.body: animate sets a look the element holds while it's on the page. Change it, and the element animates there from wherever it is, on a spring unless you set a duration: animate: {'{'} rotate: open ? 180 : 0 {'}'}. With keyframe arrays, progress (0 to 1) holds them at one point instead of playing them, so a swipe or a scroll can scrub them. With a spring, they follow it with a short lag.

size.title: Follow its content
size.body: v-animate.size eases an element to its content's new size instead of jumping.

own.title: Your own components
own.body: useMotion gives your own component the same motion as vael-ui's. Bind its transition to Vue's <Transition>. The component then follows your app's motion, animates in and out, and animates its named children with it.

states.title: States and lists
states.intro: Components also animate while they're on screen, such as on a press, a failed check or a panel opening. Lists animate items as they come and go.

press.title: Press and hover
press.body: states animates a part while the component is in a state. A plain value holds while the state is on: active: {'{'} root: {'{'} scale: '0.92' {'}'} {'}'} shrinks a button while you press it. Any element takes the same looks through v-animate: {'{'} states: {'{'} hover: {'{'} scale: 1.03 {'}'}, active: {'{'} scale: 0.97 {'}'} {'}'} {'}'}.

shake.title: A failed check
shake.body: An array plays once, as the state turns on: invalid: {'{'} root: {'{'} x: [0, -8, 8, -4, 4, 0] {'}'} {'}'} shakes a field each time it becomes invalid.

toggle.title: Open, checked, pressed
toggle.body: Accordion turns its chevron in open, and Switch squashes its thumb in active. Each component page lists its parts and states under Motion.

keyframes.title: Keyframes
keyframes.body: An array is a set of keyframes. times places each one, from 0 to 1, and easing eases each step. Pass a list of easings to give each step its own, such as a rise and then a bounce. repeat plays them again, and repeat: Infinity keeps going until the state turns off or the look changes. A step can ease on a spring: easing: ['linear', 'bouncy']. Change a loop's duration while it plays, and it speeds up or slows down from where it is.

each.title: One at a time
each.body: Some parts repeat, such as a Stepper's circles, a Dock's items or an OtpInput's cells. Each element plays its own states, so only the step that becomes current pops. Write the values as a function to use each element's index, such as for a shake that ripples cell by cell.

again.title: Play the entrance again
again.body: A component's motion takes replay too. When it changes, the component plays its initial again without remounting, such as a burst of stars on a five-star rating. appear: false stops it from playing when the component mounts.

lists.title: Lists
lists.body: Toaster, Timeline, FileUpload, SpeedDial, DataTable rows, CommandPalette rows and the Select family's chips bring new items in one after another. leaving: 'pop' lifts a leaving item out of the layout, so the rest close the gap at once. 'hold' keeps the gap until the item is gone. Write initial or exit as a function to receive {'{'} index, count {'}'} for the items arriving or leaving together, so a close can run last to first. stagger takes the same words as on v-animate (true, 'end', 'center', 'edges'), or seconds.

toasts.title: A toast that changes
toasts.body: Toaster's states play when a toast changes variant. A saving toast that ends in error can shake, and one that ends in success can pop its icon.

overlays.title: Overlays
overlays.intro: Overlays such as Dialog, Drawer, BottomSheet, Popover and Menu open and close with the motion system. They can grow out of the element that opened them, move the page with them, and change what's inside.

morph.title: Grow from the trigger
morph.body: morph: 'trigger' grows the panel out of the element that opened it, and shrinks it back into that element on close.

morphAny.title: Grow from any element
morphAny.body: Give morph a function that returns an element, such as the row you clicked. hide: false keeps the row on screen while the dialog is open.

recede.title: Move the page with it
recede.body: linked moves other elements while a Dialog, Drawer or BottomSheet is open, such as a page that recedes behind a drawer. Each entry names an element and how it looks while the overlay is open.

inner.title: The parts inside
inner.body: initial also animates a dialog's title, body and footer, so they can follow the panel in. exitOrder: 'reverse' closes them before the panel.

swap.title: Change what's inside
swap.body: Put one keyed element in the dialog and change its key. swap: 'wait' lets the old element leave before the new one arrives, and direction tells your values which way you moved.

guard.title: Ask before closing
guard.body: before-close decides whether the dialog closes. Return true to close, false to stay open, or a promise of either, such as a confirm. The dialog stays still until the answer arrives.

choreography.title: Choreography
choreography.intro: Inside a dialog or a popover, your own elements can join its motion. You name them, then time them against each other and against the panel.

after.title: One after another
after.body: Name your elements in targets, and mark them with the slot's target('name') or with v-animate:name. after: 'summary:60%' starts the rows when the summary is 60% of the way in. Elements with no component around them can wait on each other too, when they appear together: v-animate:body="{'{'} after: 'title' {'}'}".

moments.title: Moments
moments.body: after waits for a moment in another element's motion:
items: 'summary:settle': when its spring comes to rest
'panel': the component's own parts work too

steps.title: Stops along the way
steps.body: steps moves an element through a series of stops. It holds at each stop until that stop's after moment comes.

own.title: Your own timeline
own.body: An enter hook receives the parts and your targets, so one GSAP timeline can animate all of them. Return the timeline. The dialog waits for it, and stops it if you close early.

styles.title: Your app's motion
styles.intro: A motion style is one object on ConfigProvider that sets how your whole app moves: by role, by component, and with presets for your own elements.

style.title: One object for the app
style.body: A style has version: 1, a spring, and keys by role (overlay, list, press, reveal, content) or by component (dialog, toaster). A component's own motion overrides it.

presets.title: Presets
presets.body: presets names looks you can use with v-animate.rise anywhere inside the provider, so your elements move the way your components do.

parse.title: A style from outside your code
parse.body: parseMotionStyle checks a style from a settings page, a database or the network. It drops anything unsafe or unknown, and lists what it dropped in issues.

server.title: Server rendering
server.intro: Motion works on server-rendered pages: entrances start before any script, and nothing plays twice when the page hydrates.

paint.title: Before any script
paint.body: On a server-rendered page, a v-animate entrance is written into the HTML as CSS, so it plays as the page paints, before your JavaScript loads, and never again on hydration. It covers opacity, x, y, scale, blur, on a spring or a duration, built-in entrances such as v-animate.rise included. Under reduced motion it only fades.

stagger.title: A staggered list
stagger.body: A number stagger reads each element's --i: set it from v-for's index, as in :style="{'{'} '--i': index {'}'}". stagger: true spaces them by the stagger token.

later.title: What waits for JavaScript
later.body: Keyframe arrays, when: 'visible', layoutId, after, steps need the page's script, so those elements show as they are until it runs. An element named for a component (v-animate:rows) moves with its component. appear: 'later' counts the server render as the first render, so nothing there animates.

open.title: Open on load
open.body: An overlay that's open when the page loads renders open, without animating. A component's initial never plays on hydration, and a list's appear: true skips the items the server rendered.

setup.title: Nuxt and Vite
setup.body: The Nuxt module registers v-animate for you. With plain Vite SSR, set ssr: {'{'} noExternal: ['vael-ui'] {'}'} so each component's CSS comes along, and render the teleports into <body>, where overlays go. Both the VDOM and the Vapor builds render on the server and hydrate.

blocks.title: Blocks
blocks.intro: Complete pieces of interface, each built from a few vael-ui components and their motion. Copy one into your app and adapt it.
blocks.comingBody: Blocks will get their own site, blocks.vael-ui.dev. These are the first.

Bloom.title: Bloom menu
Bloom.body: A Create button grows into its menu, and the items open outward from its center.

Family.title: Wallet sheet
Family.body: A floating sheet whose views crossfade in place while it eases to each view's height.

Island.title: Dynamic island
Island.body: A pill that springs to each activity's size, with a bubble that oozes out of its side.

Feedback.title: Feedback widget
Feedback.body: The button grows into a form, and the sending state and the thank-you message swap in place.

Stack.title: Notification stack
Stack.body: Point at the stack, and the cards spread into a list.

Composer.title: Reply composer
Composer.body: Focus the box, and the tools open on a spring while the Reply button slides down to them.

ActionBar.title: Expanding action bar
ActionBar.body: Point at an action, and it expands to show its label. The bar resizes with it.

Otp.title: Verification code
Otp.body: A wrong code shakes the field, and 424242 draws a check mark.

Reveal.title: Reveal on scroll
Reveal.body: Cards rise as they scroll into view, and their numbers roll up, once.

Calendar.title: Sliding months
Calendar.body: The grid slides in the direction you moved, and the label rolls with it.

Accordion.title: Bouncy accordion
Accordion.body: Height, chevron, gaps and corners all move on one spring.

Spotlight.title: Command menu
Spotlight.body: You open it many times a day, so it keeps the quiet built-in motion.

showpieces.title: Side by side
showpieces.intro: Each showpiece in these docs was first built with GSAP, motion or vael-ui's built-in motion. Here, each one sits beside the same piece rebuilt with vael-ui motion alone. Play both the same way, and open either one's code.

Filtering.title: Filtering
Filtering.note: Filter the rows before you pass them to `data`. Here a `computed` keeps the rows that match the search and the status, and the table shows the rows it receives.

InlineEditing.title: Inline editing
InlineEditing.note: Put an `Editable` in a column’s `#cell` slot and bind it to the row’s field. Enter or leaving the cell saves, and Escape cancels. Save the change to your server in the `submit` event.

CsvExport.title: CSV export
CsvExport.note: Build the CSV from the same rows and columns the table shows, and download it as a `Blob`. Values that contain a comma, a quote or a line break are quoted.

RowGrouping.title: Row grouping
RowGrouping.note: Group the rows yourself, then pass one flat list with a header row before each group. Each header row has its own key, so CSS can style it, and its button collapses the group. Leave the columns unsorted, because sorting would move the header rows.

ColumnVisibility.title: Column visibility
ColumnVisibility.note: Keep the visible columns in a list that checkboxes change, and render each `Column` with `v-if`. When a column unmounts, the table removes it.

ValidationVeeValidate.title: Validation with vee-validate
ValidationVeeValidate.note: vee-validate holds the values and errors, and Field shows them. Pass each field’s error to `error`, and set `invalid` on its control. A field is checked when you leave it, then on every change until it’s valid. Submitting checks every field.

ValidationStandardSchema.title: Validation with a Standard Schema
ValidationStandardSchema.note: Zod, Valibot, ArkType and other Standard Schema validators all expose `~standard.validate`. Each issue’s `path` names its field, so its message goes to that Field’s `error`. This demo uses a small handwritten schema, and a Zod or Valibot schema works in its place.

PhoneMask.title: Input mask
PhoneMask.note: A mask is a small formatter on `update:modelValue`. It keeps only the digits and formats them as (555) 123-4567, so typing, pasting and deleting give the same result. Send the digits to your server.

CharacterCounter.title: Character counter
CharacterCounter.note: Show the length of the `v-model` value in the `#end` slot. `maxlength` stops input at the limit, and `aria-describedby` links the count to the field for screen readers.

RangePresets.title: Range presets
RangePresets.note: Put buttons for common ranges next to a range picker. Each button builds a range with `start` and `end` and sets it as the `v-model` value. You can still pick dates by hand.

ClosableTabs.title: Closable tabs
ClosableTabs.note: Render each tab yourself, with a close button inside it. When you close the selected tab, the tab to its right is selected, or the one to its left if it was last. Focus moves to that tab, so keyboard users keep their place. Delete or Backspace closes the focused tab.

JumpToPage.title: Jump to page
JumpToPage.note: Put an `InputNumber` next to the pagination for long lists. `min` and `max` keep the number within the page count. Press Enter or leave the field to go to that page.

ImagePreviews.title: Image previews
ImagePreviews.note: Create an object URL for each image and show it in the `#item` slot. An object URL keeps its file in memory until you revoke it. Revoke each URL when its image is removed, and revoke the rest when the component unmounts.

DraggableDialog.title: Draggable dialog
DraggableDialog.note: Drag the header to move the dialog. Pointer capture keeps the drag going when the pointer leaves the header. With the grip button focused, the arrow keys move it 10 px, or 50 px with Shift. The dialog stays inside the window and opens centered again.
